conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to do a quick check-in with you today using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week since your baby arrived. Nothing you share will leave this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. When we’re done I’ll tally things up and we can talk about gentle next steps if they’re needed. Ready to start?  

First, in the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when life feels a little chaotic?

Honestly? I can still laugh sometimes—like when the baby lets out a little milk-sneeze or my husband does his silly dinosaur voices—but it feels muted, like I’m hearing myself chuckle from another room. Most days I have to remind myself to smile, and even when something is genuinely funny, the laugh fades fast and I’m right back to feeling flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yes. I still laugh—like when my sister sent that ridiculous meme about diaper explosions—but it feels kind of forced, and the laugh doesn’t last. It’s like the joy gets sucked out almost right away, and then I’m just tired again.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to—like I’ll tell myself, “It’ll be fun to take the baby for a walk tomorrow,” or “Maybe I’ll feel like baking again this weekend.” But when the moment comes, it just feels… flat. I still go through the motions, hoping the enjoyment will show up, but mostly I’m just going from one feeding to the next.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Last night the baby was fussier than usual and I kept thinking maybe it’s because I drank that extra cup of coffee, or I didn’t hold him long enough after the feeding. Rationally I know babies just cry, but I still get this little stab of “I must’ve done something wrong.” It’s not constant, but it pops up a few times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get hit with waves of worry, mostly about the baby—like if he’s breathing when he’s napping or whether that tiny cough means he’s getting sick. There’s no real reason, but my mind races anyway. It’s not all day, maybe a few times a day, and it settles once I check on him, but those moments feel tight in my chest.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice this week I’ll be rocking him at 3 a.m. and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel shaky, like something awful is about to happen—even though we’re both safe in the nursery. It passes in a few minutes, but it leaves me jittery and I have to sit down and breathe slowly so I don’t wake the baby with my own trembling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. It feels like the laundry and bottles and texts I haven’t answered just pile up, and I’ll stare at the mess and think, “I can’t keep up.” I’m not falling apart, but I get that heavy, sinking feeling—like I’m wading through knee-deep water—maybe three or four times a week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but several nights this week I’ve laid down exhausted and then my brain just starts circling—did I sterilize the pump parts, is he gaining enough weight, will I ever feel like myself again? I finally drift off, but it takes forever, and when he wakes for feeds I’m still wired. I’m getting maybe four broken hours, if that.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah... I get waves of sadness most days, usually in the late afternoon when everything feels dull and the house is quiet except for baby noises. It’s not all-day despair, but I’ll find myself tearing up while folding onesies or just staring out the window feeling heavy. It lifts a bit after dinner, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once or twice this week. One night I was nursing at 2 a.m., the room felt so quiet and lonely, and a couple tears just slipped out. It wasn’t a big sob, more like a slow leak, and it stopped once he finished feeding.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and low, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

You've painted a moving picture of new motherhood right now: laughing at your sister's meme yet feeling the joy slip away, planning walks that feel flat by daylight, and sitting up at 3 a.m. with racing heart and shaky hands while the rest of the house sleeps. You described waves of afternoon sadness, heavy "knee-deep water" days, and nights where your mind spins through pump parts and worries instead of letting you rest. Through it all you're caring beautifully for your baby, even when your own emotional tank feels close to empty.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughs occasionally but describes joy as fleeting and laughter as forced, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes anticipatory planning that consistently yields no pleasure—"flat" affect and joyless routine align with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes recurring, intrusive worries about the baby's well-being without real cause, happening multiple times daily and causing physical tension, aligning with the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected panic episodes (racing heart, trembling, dread) that fit "scared or panicky for no very good reason" and occur several times in the past week, aligning with the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent (3-4×/week) overwhelm with household tasks and a heavy, sinking feeling, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports several nights of difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeable daily waves of sadness that recur and cause tearfulness, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 17 (≥14 indicates probable major depression). She endorses core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: <sym>depressed mood</sym> most days, <sym>markedly diminished interest/pleasure</sym> (<quote>hoping the enjoyment will show up</quote>), <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness/guilt</sym> (<quote>I must've done something wrong</quote>), <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>psychomotor agitation</sym>/anxiety. <sym>Recurrent panic-like episodes</sym> and <sym>worry</sym> suggest comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. No suicidal ideation (Q10 score 0). Score places her well above routine-support threshold, meeting mhGAP-IG guidance for urgent <med>mental health referral</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within one week
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options (therapy ± medication) safe for breastfeeding
3. Begin weekly <med>cognitive-behavioural</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> sessions focused on postpartum issues
4. Plan daily 20-minute outdoor walks and 5-minute breathing breaks to reduce <sym>anxiety</sym> and improve <sym>mood</sym>
5. Share local <med>postpartum support group</med> contacts and 24-hour parent helpline numbers
6. Encourage partner/family to handle one night feeding so she can obtain a 4-hour stretch of sleep
7. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks to track symptom change
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Structured Note

Patient: Postpartum mother (≤12 mo); responses self-reported.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Depressed mood: daily waves of sadness, tearfulness 2×/week, low afternoon mood.  
- Anhedonia: anticipates but does not experience enjoyment; laughter feels forced.  
- Guilt / self-blame: recurrent, situation-specific, 3–4×/week.  
- Anxiety: situational worries about infant safety, chest tightness, 3×/day.  
- Panic symptoms: abrupt racing heart/shakiness, 2×/week, 3 a.m., resolves <5 min.  
- Feeling overwhelmed: “knee-deep water” sensation, 3–4×/week.  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia with rumination, ~4 broken hrs/night, several nights/week.

Safety  
Denies any self-harm thoughts (Q10 “No—never”).

Pattern Summary  
Persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, and anxious hyper-vigilance meet screening threshold for possible postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. No current suicidal ideation; no psychotic features reported.

Screening Significance  
Elevated risk for major postpartum depressive episode and/or anxiety disorder; warrants formal clinical interview (EPDS / PHQ-9 / GAD-7) and possible referral to outpatient perinatal mental health specialty.
